p: The Kidron runs between the city and the Mount of Olives. It carries water only in the rainy season.
b: The Greek cheimarros means a "winter stream": a ravine that flows only after winter rains, what Arabs call a wadi. The Kidron separates the Temple hill from the Mount of Olives. King David crossed it weeping when his son Absalom drove him out of Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15:23), just after a counselor he trusted had turned against him (2 Samuel 15:31). Early readers saw Jesus walking David's road. Matthew and Mark name the place Gethsemane, "oil press" (Matthew 26:36; Mark 14:32); Luke says the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39). Only John calls it a garden.
orig: πέραν τοῦ χειμάρρου τοῦ Κεδρών (peran tou cheimarrou tou Kedrōn)

p: The passion begins in a garden, ends with a burial in a garden, and Easter morning meets a "gardener."
b: John alone opens and closes the passion in a garden (kēpos): the arrest here, the tomb "in the garden" (19:41), and Mary Magdalene taking the risen Jesus for the man who kept the garden (20:15). Many readers, from early Christian writers to modern literary critics, hear an echo of Eden, where the first humans failed in a garden (Genesis 2:8; 3:8). John never says so outright, and the Greek of Genesis uses a different word (paradeisos), so the link is a reader's connection, not a stated claim. Others see a simple fact: Jerusalem's slopes were full of walled orchards and olive groves.

p: The verb means "hand over." John uses it for Judas, the priests, Pilate, and finally for Jesus himself.
b: Paradidōmi means to hand someone or something over to another. English Bibles usually say "betray" for Judas, which is the sense, but the word has no meaning of treachery in itself. Using "hand over" lets the reader follow a chain in John: Judas hands Jesus over to the authorities (18:2, 5), they hand him to Pilate (18:30, 35), Pilate hands him over to be crucified (19:16), and at the end Jesus himself "handed over his spirit" (19:30). The last link turns the chain around: no one takes his life from him; he gives it (10:18).

p: A speira was a Roman unit of up to 600 men. Only John puts Roman troops in the garden.
b: A speira (Latin cohors) was a tenth of a legion, nominally 600 soldiers, and its commander was a chiliarchos, a tribune (18:12). John does not mean all 600 came, but he does mean Romans: the same words are used of Roman units in Acts 21:31 and 27:1. Matthew, Mark and Luke speak only of a crowd sent by the chief priests and elders (Mark 14:43). Views: (1) John is right, and the arrest was planned with the governor's garrison from the start, which fits a crowded Passover and a feared revolt; (2) John uses military words loosely for Temple forces; (3) John adds Rome to show that the whole "world" (15:18) came out against Jesus. Raymond Brown thought a small Roman detachment historically possible.

a: guards sent by the chief priests and the Pharisees
p: These were the Temple police, the same "guards" who once came back without arresting Jesus.
b: The hypēretai were attendants and guards who served the chief priests and the Temple. The same group was sent to arrest Jesus at the Feast of Booths and came back empty-handed (7:32, 45–46). John often pairs the chief priests and the Pharisees as the leaders who act against Jesus (7:32; 11:47, 57). Historically the priests ran the Temple, while the Pharisees were a lay movement known for careful keeping of the law; John's pairing may reflect his own time, after AD 70, when the Pharisees' heirs led the synagogues his readers had left. The same guards appear with the Roman cohort in 18:12, where John calls them "the guards of the Jews."

t: "I am": an ordinary phrase, or the divine name?
p: Greek egō eimi can mean "It's me." But here it knocks an armed crowd to the ground.
b: In everyday Greek egō eimi just means "I am the one" or "It's me," as the man born blind says in 9:9. But John uses the phrase on purpose. Jesus has said "unless you believe that I am" (8:24) and "before Abraham came to be, I am" (8:58), which echo the Greek of Isaiah, where God says egō eimi of himself (Isaiah 43:10, 25), and God's naming of himself to Moses (Exodus 3:14). The phrase sounds three times in this scene (18:5, 6, 8), and the soldiers' fall (18:6) shows the reader what it carries. Some scholars think John means only "I am he"; most think he intends both senses at once.

a: they stepped backward and fell to the ground
p: Only John tells it. Readers have seen a miracle, plain shock, or a scene shaped by the Psalms.
b: Three readings: (1) A display of divine power. The crowd falls before the divine name, as people fall before God's glory (Ezekiel 1:28; Daniel 10:9). Jesus is not captured; he lets himself be taken (10:18). This is the traditional view, from Origen and John Chrysostom on. (2) A natural event. The front ranks pulled back in surprise at a man who walked straight up to them, and some stumbled. (3) A scene told in the words of the Psalms, where the righteous one's attackers fall: "it was they who tripped and went down" (Psalm 27:2; compare Psalm 35:4). These are not exclusive. John's point is that Jesus is in control of his "hour."

a: "I did not lose a single one of those you have given me."
p: John quotes Jesus' own prayer and treats it as fulfilled, the way he treats the Old Testament.
b: The words come from Jesus' prayer (17:12) and his promises in 6:39 and 10:28. John uses the formula "so that... would come true" (hina plērōthē) here for Jesus' word, exactly as he does for Scripture in 19:24 and 19:36; he does it again in 18:32. For John, Jesus' words carry the authority of Scripture. There is also a shift: in 17:12 Jesus means losing them to final ruin; here John applies the words to keeping them safe from arrest that night. The bodily rescue is a sign of the deeper one.

p: All four Gospels tell of the cut-off ear. Only John names the swordsman and the slave.
b: Matthew, Mark and Luke say only that someone standing by struck "the high priest's slave" (Mark 14:47); Luke adds that it was the right ear and that Jesus healed it (Luke 22:50–51). John names Peter and the slave. Malchus was a known name, common among the Nabataean Arabs (Malichus). Some scholars see the names as later storytelling, since tradition tends to fill in names; others, such as Richard Bauckham, think they show John's source knew the high priest's household (18:15–16, 26). Either way, naming Peter here sets up his denials in front of Malchus's relative (18:26).

a: The cup the Father has handed me, am I not to drink it?
p: John has no prayer in Gethsemane, but he knows its words: the cup the Father gives.
b: In the other Gospels Jesus prays in the garden that the cup might pass from him (Mark 14:36). John has no such scene; his Jesus has already refused to ask to be saved "from this hour" (12:27). Here the cup is accepted, not prayed against. In the Old Testament the cup is often God's anger that the wicked must drink: "the LORD holds a cup in his hand... all the wicked of the earth" will drain it (Psalm 75:8; compare Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Christian readers have long understood Jesus as drinking that cup in place of others.
r: Mark 14:36; Matthew 26:39; Luke 22:42; 12:27; Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15; Mark 10:38

a: with the guards of the Jews
p: Here "the Jews" means the Temple authorities who sent these guards (18:3), not the Jewish people.
b: In 18:3 the same guards were "sent by the chief priests and the Pharisees"; now John calls them "the guards of the Jews." So in this passage "the Jews" is shorthand for the Jerusalem leaders who ran the Temple. Jesus and all his disciples were Jews too. Reading the word this way, as John's own usage shows, keeps the story from being heard as a charge against a whole people.

p: Annas had been high priest years before. Caiaphas, his son-in-law, held the office from about AD 18 to 36.
b: Annas son of Seth was made high priest by the Romans in AD 6 and removed in AD 15, but he remained the head of the most powerful priestly family. Josephus says five of his sons became high priest, which no one else achieved (Jewish Antiquities 20.198). Caiaphas held the office from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long term that suggests he worked well with the Roman governors. "High priest in that year" does not mean the post changed yearly; it means "in that fateful year" (11:49, 51). In 1990 a decorated bone box inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas" was found in a family tomb in Jerusalem; many scholars think it held his bones.

a: had given the Jews his advice
p: The advice was given to the council (11:47–53), so "the Jews" here means the council's members.
b: John looks back to 11:47–53, where the chief priests and Pharisees met in council and Caiaphas told them that one man should die for the people. "The Jews" in this verse are the members of that council, not the people of Jerusalem, many of whom had come to believe in Jesus (11:45; 12:11). Throughout the passion John uses the word for the leaders who acted against Jesus.

a: it is better for one man to die on behalf of the people
p: John reminds the reader of 11:50: the high priest spoke more truly than he knew.
b: John points back to the council meeting after Lazarus was raised (11:47–53). Caiaphas meant a political calculation: let one troublemaker die so that Rome does not destroy the nation. John says that as high priest he "prophesied" without knowing it that Jesus would die for the nation, "and not just for the nation" (11:51–52). The reminder tells the reader that the verdict was decided before the questioning begins.

t: The disciple known to the high priest
p: He is not named. Many think he is the disciple Jesus loved; others think he is someone else.
b: This unnamed disciple is "known to" the high priest, well enough to speak to the gatekeeper and bring Peter in. Because "the other disciple" is later used of the disciple Jesus loved (20:2–3), many readers identify the two. But how could a Galilean fisherman such as John son of Zebedee be known in the high priest's house? Answers include: his family sold fish to the household (a late tradition); he came from a priestly family (Polycrates of Ephesus, about AD 190, says John "wore the priestly plate," in Eusebius, Church History 5.24); or the Beloved Disciple was not a Galilean at all but a Jerusalem follower. On who he was, see 13:23 and the topic page.

p: In the garden Jesus says "I am." In the courtyard Peter says "I am not."
b: Peter's answer is two Greek words, ouk eimi, the exact negative of Jesus' egō eimi (18:5). John sets the scenes side by side on purpose: outside, Jesus faces soldiers and owns his name; inside, Peter faces a slave girl and disowns his. He says it again in 18:25. John the Baptist had also said "I am not" (1:20–21), and spoke the truth. Peter says it falsely, as Jesus had warned (13:38).

p: The word appears only twice in the New Testament: here, where Peter denies Jesus, and at 21:9, where Jesus restores him.
b: Anthrakia, a fire of charcoal, is found in the New Testament only here and in 21:9. Peter denies Jesus three times while warming himself at one; after the resurrection he finds Jesus cooking breakfast over another, and there Jesus asks him three times, "Do you love me?" (21:15–17). Few readers think the repetition is an accident. The detail also fits the season: Jerusalem stands about 2,500 feet up, and spring nights at Passover can be cold.

t: Which high priest? John and the night trial
p: Annas questions Jesus here, though Caiaphas held office. John has no night trial before the council.
b: Annas is called "the high priest" because former high priests kept the title, as Luke 3:2 and Acts 4:6 also show. John describes a private questioning at Annas's house, then sends Jesus to Caiaphas (18:24) without telling what happened there. Matthew and Mark describe a night session of the council (the Sanhedrin) before Caiaphas, with witnesses and a charge of blasphemy (Mark 14:53–65). Views: (1) John fills in a hearing the others leave out; (2) John put the council's decision earlier (11:47–53), so that his whole Gospel works as the trial; (3) the Synoptic night trial is a later shaping of events, and John's informal hearing is closer to what happened, a view held by many historians, including E. P. Sanders and Paula Fredriksen.

a: I have spoken to the world in the open
p: Jesus answers a question about his teaching by pointing to his public life.
b: Jesus refuses to be treated as the leader of a secret movement. He taught "in synagogue," as at Capernaum (6:59), and in the Temple courts (7:14, 28; 8:20; 10:23). The other Gospels record the same protest at his arrest: he had taught in the Temple day after day (Mark 14:49). The words also recall God's claim in Isaiah 45:19 that he had not spoken in secret. A case was to rest on witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6), and the Mishnah's later rules for trials say the same, which may be why Jesus says, "Ask the people who heard."

p: A guard hits Jesus for speaking that way to the high priest. Jesus answers with a legal challenge.
b: The guard may have had in mind the law "do not curse a leader of your people" (Exodus 22:28), the verse Paul quotes when he is struck at the high priest's order and then apologizes (Acts 23:2–5). Jesus does not apologize. He asks for evidence: if he spoke badly, let someone testify to it. The scene shows the hearing for what it is. Augustine contrasted this with Jesus' teaching to "turn the other cheek" (Matthew 5:39): Jesus does not hit back, but he does not stay silent about injustice either. Isaiah's servant also gave his cheeks to those who struck him (Isaiah 50:6).

a: So Annas sent him, tied up, to Caiaphas the high priest
t: An awkward order, and a Syriac fix
p: Annas sends Jesus to Caiaphas only after the questioning. One early Syriac copy moves this verse to smooth it.
b: If Caiaphas was "the high priest" in 18:19, why does Annas send Jesus to him afterward? Most scholars think 18:19–23 is Annas's hearing and that the title is used loosely. Some ancient readers tried to repair the order. The Sinaitic Syriac, a Syriac copy of the Gospels from about AD 400, puts 18:24 right after 18:13 and rearranges the Peter scenes around it, so that the questioning happens before Caiaphas; a few Greek manuscripts and Cyril of Alexandria also place 18:24 after 18:13 (reported by Metzger). The order of all the other Greek manuscripts, which every modern edition follows, is the harder reading and almost certainly the original.

p: Jesus had said Peter would deny him three times before the rooster crowed (13:38).
b: The rooster fulfills Jesus' warning at supper (13:38; Matthew 26:34; Mark 14:30; Luke 22:34). Mark has the rooster crow twice (Mark 14:72). "Cockcrow" was also a name for the third watch of the night, about midnight to 3 a.m. (Mark 13:35). John does not describe Peter's weeping, as the others do (Matthew 26:75; Luke 22:62). He saves Peter's story for chapter 21, where three questions answer three denials.

p: The governor's headquarters in Jerusalem, probably Herod's old palace on the city's west side.
b: The Roman governor lived at Caesarea on the coast and came up to Jerusalem at festivals to keep order. His headquarters there, the praetorium, was either Herod the Great's palace near today's Jaffa Gate, where Philo and Josephus say governors stayed, or the Antonia fortress beside the Temple, the traditional site on the Via Dolorosa. Most archaeologists now favor Herod's palace. John's story moves back and forth between inside, where Pilate questions Jesus, and outside, where the accusers wait: seven scenes in all (18:28–19:16). See the chapter page.

p: Entering a Gentile home was thought to make a Jew ritually unclean, which would keep him from the Passover.
b: The Mishnah, written down about AD 200, says that "the dwelling places of Gentiles are unclean" (Mishnah Ohalot 18:7), probably for fear that a dead infant had been buried there, since contact with the dead made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11), too long to keep the Passover (Numbers 9:6). Peter says in Acts 10:28 that a Jew was not supposed to enter a Gentile's home. John's irony is sharp: these men guard their purity while handing an innocent man over to death. Jewish readers rightly note that keeping the purity laws was faithful obedience; the irony is aimed at these men, not at the law.

a: so that they could eat the Passover
t: When was the Passover? John and the other Gospels
p: In John the Passover meal is still ahead on the day Jesus dies. In Mark the Last Supper was the Passover meal.
b: In Matthew, Mark and Luke the Last Supper is the Passover meal (Mark 14:12–16), so Jesus dies on the first day of the festival. In John the priests have not yet eaten the Passover, and Jesus dies on "Preparation Day for the Passover" (19:14), the afternoon the lambs were slaughtered. Views: (1) John has the date right, and the Synoptics made the last meal a Passover (John P. Meier and many historians); (2) the Synoptics have it right, and John moved the day to show Jesus as the Lamb (1:29; 19:36), as Joachim Jeremias argued; (3) both are right: "eat the Passover" here means the festival's other sacred meals that week (D. A. Carson), or groups followed different calendars (Annie Jaubert, from the solar calendar of the Dead Sea Scrolls). Astronomical tables (Colin Humphreys and W. G. Waddington) put Nisan 14 on a Friday in AD 30 and AD 33, which fits John. The question is still open.

p: The Roman prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36. Writers outside the Bible describe a harsh ruler.
b: Pilate governed Judea for ten years. A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 names him "[Pon]tius Pilatus, [Praef]ectus Iuda[ea]e," prefect of Judea. Philo calls him stubborn and cruel (On the Embassy to Gaius 299–305), and Josephus tells of riots he provoked with Roman standards in Jerusalem and with Temple money taken for an aqueduct (Jewish War 2.169–177). Tacitus names him as the one who executed "Christus" (Annals 15.44). In John he is shrewd and afraid at once. Some historians think the Gospels soften his guilt to blame the Jewish leaders; others, such as Helen Bond, say his maneuvering fits a governor playing the crowd and the priests against each other.

p: The speakers are the accusers who brought Jesus to the Praetorium: the chief priests and their people (18:35).
b: The ones who answer Pilate are the men who led Jesus from Caiaphas to the Praetorium (18:28). Pilate himself identifies them in 18:35: "It was your nation and the chief priests who handed you to me." In 19:6 John names those who shout as "the chief priests and the guards." In the trial scenes "the Jews" means this group of accusers, a small circle of Temple leaders and their staff, not the Jewish people as a whole.

a: "We are not permitted to kill anyone."
t: Could the Jewish council carry out a death sentence?
p: A long debate: had Rome taken away the council's right to execute?
b: Views: (1) No: Rome kept capital cases for the governor, as in other provinces. A rabbinic tradition says that forty years before the Temple fell the council stopped judging capital cases (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 41a), and Josephus says the high priest Ananus, Annas's son, was removed after he had James the brother of Jesus stoned while no governor was in the land (Jewish Antiquities 20.200–203). A. N. Sherwin-White defended this view from Roman law. (2) Yes, in some cases (Jean Juster; Paul Winter, On the Trial of Jesus): a surviving Temple inscription warns Gentiles that entering the inner courts means death, and Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:58). (3) The words mean "not at the festival" or "not by crucifixion." Most scholars hold view (1) for Judea under the prefects.

a: the sort of death he would die
p: Stoning would not fulfill Jesus' word. He had said he would be "lifted up."
b: John points to 12:32–33, where Jesus spoke of being "lifted up from the earth," and John explained that this showed the kind of death he would die; see also 3:14 and 8:28. A Jewish court's penalty for blasphemy was stoning (Leviticus 24:16; compare John 8:59; John 10:31). Roman crucifixion is the death that "lifts up," like the bronze snake Moses set on a pole: "he would look at the bronze snake and live" (Numbers 21:9). Peter's death is described with the same phrase in 21:19.

a: "So you are the King of the Jews?"
p: In Roman ears "King of the Jews" meant a rebel. In all four Gospels Pilate's first question is this one.
b: All four Gospels open Pilate's questioning with the same words (Matthew 27:11; Mark 15:2; Luke 23:3). Rome had given the title "king of the Jews" to Herod the Great; anyone else who claimed it was a rebel against Caesar, and several would-be kings had risen in Judea after Herod's death (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 17.271–285). The title follows Jesus to the sign on the cross (19:19). "Messiah" was a Jewish word of hope; to a Roman it sounded like a political threat, which is why the accusers press it (19:12).

a: My kingdom does not come from this world
t: Not "of this world": where it comes from, not where it is
p: The Greek ek means "from." Jesus speaks of the source of his rule, not of a purely inner or heavenly kingdom.
b: The familiar "My kingdom is not of this world" is often heard as "my kingdom has nothing to do with this world." But ek tou kosmou means "out of, from" this world: its source and character, not its location. Jesus uses the same phrase of his disciples, who are in the world but not "from" it (17:14–16). His kingdom does not get its power the way Caesar's does, by soldiers; that is why his "guards" (the same word as the Temple guards of 18:3) do not fight. The verse has been used to keep churches out of politics and, on the other side, to argue that Christ's rule judges every earthly power. See the topic on church and state.
orig: οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου (ouk estin ek tou kosmou toutou)

p: Jesus, himself a Jew, means the authorities who had him arrested, not his own people.
b: Jesus says that if his kingdom were of this world, his followers would have fought to keep him from being "handed over to the Jews." Since Jesus and his followers were Jews, the word cannot mean the Jewish people here. It means the Temple authorities whose guards came for him in the garden (18:3, 12). John's shorthand is clear in context, but read carelessly it has fed the false idea that "the Jews" as a people were Jesus' enemies.

a: You are the one saying I am a king
p: Jesus neither denies the title nor accepts Pilate's meaning of it.
b: Sy legeis, "you say," appears in the trial scenes of all four Gospels (Matthew 27:11; Mark 15:2; Luke 23:3). It is not a flat "yes" or "no." It means something like "That is your word for it." Jesus is a king, but not the kind Pilate has in mind, and he goes on to redefine kingship: he came to bear witness to the truth. Some read the words as a question ("Do you say that I am a king?"); reading them as a guarded yes is far more common. Paul later calls this Jesus' "good confession in front of Pontius Pilate" (1 Timothy 6:13).
orig: Σὺ λέγεις ὅτι βασιλεύς εἰμι (sy legeis hoti basileus eimi)
r: Matthew 26:25; Matthew 26:64; Matthew 27:11; Mark 15:2; Luke 22:70; Luke 23:3; 1 Timothy 6:13

p: Pilate does not wait for an answer. Readers have heard cynicism, weariness, mockery or honest curiosity.
b: Pilate walks out before Jesus can reply. Readers have taken his words as: (1) a cynic's sneer at idealists, as in Francis Bacon's essay "Of Truth" (1625), which begins with "jesting Pilate" who "would not stay for an answer"; (2) a politician's impatience with philosophy; (3) a sincere but confused question. John's irony is that the one who called himself the truth (14:6) stands in front of him. In John, truth (alētheia) is not mainly an idea but God's faithful reality, made known in Jesus (1:14, 17; 8:32).

a: went back out to the Jews
p: The people waiting outside are the accusers who would not enter the Praetorium (18:28).
b: Pilate keeps moving between Jesus inside and the accusers outside, who would not come in for fear of becoming unclean (18:28). Those outside are the same group each time: the chief priests and their guards, as 19:6 makes plain. John never mentions a crowd of ordinary people in his trial scene, unlike Mark (Mark 15:8–15). When the reader hears "the Jews" here, the right picture is a delegation of leaders, not a nation.

p: The Gospels mention a custom of freeing one prisoner at Passover. No source outside them mentions it.
b: Matthew and Mark call it the governor's custom (Matthew 27:15; Mark 15:6); John calls it the people's. No Roman or Jewish source outside the Gospels describes such an amnesty. Some point to the Mishnah's rule that a Passover lamb may be slaughtered for someone whom the authorities have promised to bring out of prison (Mishnah Pesahim 8:6), which assumes releases at Passover happened; others note Roman examples of governors freeing prisoners when a crowd demanded it. Skeptical scholars think the custom is a storytelling device; others think it a local practice too small to be recorded elsewhere.

p: Lēstēs can mean a robber, but Josephus uses it for armed rebels against Rome. Mark says Barabbas was in an uprising.
b: The KJV's "robber" is the usual meaning of lēstēs, but Josephus uses the word again and again for rebels and guerrilla fighters in Judea (Jewish War 2.253–254). Mark says Barabbas was in prison with rebels who had killed people during an uprising (Mark 15:7). So the accusers choose a violent rebel over a king whose guards do not fight (18:36). The name Barabbas is Aramaic for "son of the father" (bar abba). Some manuscripts of Matthew 27:16–17 call him "Jesus Barabbas," a reading Origen knew and this site's Matthew follows, which would sharpen the choice. Jesus used the same word for the thieves and bandits who climb into the sheepfold (10:1, 8).

p: A Roman flogging used a whip of leather straps weighted with bone or metal. In John it comes in the middle of the trial.
b: Romans used several grades of beating. The worst, given before crucifixion, used a whip (flagellum) of leather thongs with bits of bone or metal, and could expose bone or kill. In Mark and Matthew the flogging follows the sentence (Mark 15:15). In John, Pilate orders it before any verdict, apparently hoping a bloodied prisoner will satisfy the crowd (19:4–6); Luke has Pilate offer to "teach him a lesson and set him free" (Luke 23:16). Some scholars think John describes a lighter beating as a warning; others think John moved the scourging to the center of his trial story for effect.
r: Mark 15:15; Matthew 27:26; Luke 23:16; Luke 23:22; Isaiah 50:6; Isaiah 53:5

a: wove a crown out of thorny branches
p: A mock crown for a mock king. It may have imitated the spiky crowns of rulers on coins.
b: The soldiers are acting out a coronation: crown, royal purple, acclamation ("Hail!") and blows in place of homage. H. St. J. Hart argued that the crown was made of long date-palm spines pointing outward, imitating the rayed crown of rulers on coins, rather than a cap of thorns pressed in to cause pain; others think it was both mockery and torture. Christian readers have connected the thorns with the curse on the ground after Adam's sin, "Thorn and thistle it will sprout for you" (Genesis 3:18), a link that goes back to the early church; the Gospel does not draw it.

p: Pilate means "Look at this pitiful man." John's readers hear more.
b: In Latin, Ecce homo, a favorite subject of painters. Readings: (1) Pity or contempt: Pilate shows a broken man to say "This is no threat." (2) Irony: Pilate unknowingly presents "the Man," the Son of Man, enthroned in suffering; compare his later "Look at your king!" (19:14). (3) Echo: some hear Zechariah 6:12 in the Greek, "Look, a man whose name is the Branch," a royal promise; the Greek words differ, so the echo is uncertain. (4) Some church fathers read it as Pilate showing true humanity: the Word made flesh (1:14) in its lowest form.

p: The accusers now give the religious charge: he made himself God's Son. In Jewish law that was blasphemy.
b: Until now the charge before Pilate was political ("King of the Jews"). Here the accusers name what had offended them all along: he made himself "God's Son," equal with God (5:18; 10:33). The law in mind is Leviticus 24:16, against speaking the Name with contempt, which carried the death penalty. Jewish scholars point out that the Mishnah later defined blasphemy narrowly, as pronouncing the divine name itself (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:5), so whether Jesus' words met the legal test is debated. "The Jews" here are the chief priests and their guards (19:6); see the topic on "the Jews" in John.

a: Pilate grew more afraid than ever
p: To a Roman, a "son of god" might be a divine man. Pilate's fear is religious as well as political.
b: Greeks and Romans told of sons of gods walking among people, and some of Paul's hearers took him and Barnabas for gods (Acts 14:11). The emperor himself was called "son of the deified one" (divi filius). So "he made himself out to be God's Son" could alarm a superstitious governor. Matthew adds that Pilate's wife sent word of a troubling dream (Matthew 27:19). John says Pilate was "more" afraid, though he has not mentioned fear before; some take it to mean "very afraid."

p: Pilate means "What land are you from?" In John, the question of Jesus' origin is the question of who he is.
b: Luke tells that Pilate, learning Jesus was from Galilee, sent him to Herod (Luke 23:6–7). In John the question runs through the whole Gospel: the crowd claims to know where Jesus comes from (7:27), the Pharisees say they do not (9:29), and Jesus says, "I know the place I came from and the place I am going" (8:14). He comes "from above" (3:31; 8:23). His silence here matches the servant of Isaiah 53:7, who did not open his mouth, and the silence before Pilate in Mark 15:5.

p: The same word Jesus used for being "born from above" (3:3). Pilate's power comes from God, and he answers for it.
b: Anōthen means "from above" (3:31; 19:23) and, in 3:3, both "from above" and "again." Jesus tells the man who boasts of power over life and death that his power is borrowed from God, as Daniel told Nebuchadnezzar that "the Most High rules" over human kingdoms (Daniel 4:17). Paul says the same of all governing authority (Romans 13:1). The verse has been read two ways in debates on church and state: rulers rule by God's appointment, so obey them; and rulers answer to God, so they can be judged. Calvin read it as both.

a: the one who handed me over to you
p: Most think Jesus means Caiaphas, who handed him to Pilate. Some think Judas. Either way, guilt has degrees.
b: The singular "the one who handed me over" fits Judas, who is called by that title throughout (18:2, 5). But it was Caiaphas and the chief priests who handed Jesus to Pilate (18:30, 35), so most commentators, such as Raymond Brown and D. A. Carson, think Jesus means the high priest, perhaps standing for the authorities. The point is that Pilate is not innocent ("greater" means he too has sin), but the one who knew the Scriptures and acted on purpose bears more. Christians have used the verse to teach that sins differ in weight, a theme also in Luke 12:47–48.

p: John has already named those who shout: "the chief priests and the guards" (19:6).
b: The shouts in 19:6, 19:12 and 19:15 come from one group, and John names it twice: "the chief priests and the guards" (19:6) and "the chief priests" (19:15). "The Jews" in this verse is John's shorthand for them. It is these Temple leaders who threaten Pilate with Caesar's displeasure, a threat with real force, since Pilate's career depended on the emperor's favor.

p: A real title of honor for loyal officials. Losing it could end a career, or a life.
b: Amicus Caesaris, "Friend of Caesar," was an honor given to senators and officials close to the emperor. The threat is clear: if Pilate frees a man who claims to be king, they will report him to Tiberius, who was known for treason trials. Some historians connect this with the fall in AD 31 of Sejanus, a powerful minister who may have been Pilate's patron, after which friends of Sejanus were purged; that link is possible but unproven. In the end the accusers win by forcing Pilate to choose between Jesus and Caesar.

a: He took his seat on the judge's platform
t: Who sat on the judgment seat?
p: The verb can also mean "he seated him." A few readers think Pilate put Jesus on the judge's seat in mockery.
b: Kathizō can be intransitive ("he sat") or transitive ("he seated someone"). Most translations and commentators read "Pilate sat down" as judge, which is the normal sense and fits Matthew 27:19. But the second-century Gospel of Peter says the crowd "sat him on a seat of judgment" and mocked him, and Justin Martyr (First Apology 35) tells it the same way. Some modern scholars think John meant both: Pilate sits as judge, while the reader knows the real judge is Jesus, to whom the Father has given all judgment (5:22, 27).

p: John's "Hebrew" usually means Aramaic, the spoken language of Judea. Gabbatha may mean "the height."
b: When John says "in Hebrew," the words he gives (Gabbatha, Golgotha, Rabboni) are Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in the land, a sister of Hebrew. Gabbatha probably means "the ridge" or "the height," a raised platform, while the Greek name Lithostrōtos means "paved with stones." The striking stone pavement shown to visitors under the Ecce Homo convent in Jerusalem dates from the time of Emperor Hadrian, a century later, so it is not the place. If the Praetorium was Herod's palace, the platform stood on the city's high western hill.

p: The day before a Sabbath or festival. Here: the day before the Passover meal, or the Friday of Passover week.
b: Paraskeuē means "preparation." Jews used it for the day before the Sabbath, Friday, and in later Greek it became the name for Friday. Mark says Jesus died on "the Day of Preparation, which is the day before the Sabbath" (Mark 15:42). John's phrase "Preparation of the Passover" most naturally means the day before the Passover meal, the afternoon when lambs were slaughtered in the Temple (Exodus 12:6), which agrees with 18:28. Those who harmonize John with the Synoptics read it as "the Friday of Passover week." See the note on 18:28.

a: The time was about the sixth hour
t: The sixth hour and Mark's third hour
p: Counted from sunrise, the sixth hour is about noon. Mark puts the crucifixion at the third hour, about 9 a.m.
b: Mark says it was "the third hour" when they crucified him (Mark 15:25), while in John the sentence is still being given at "about the sixth hour." Suggested answers: (1) John counts from midnight, Roman civil style, so 6 a.m.; but John's other hours (1:39; 4:6) fit counting from dawn. (2) Both are rough: people told time in three-hour blocks, and "about" a morning hour could fall between 9 and noon (Carson). (3) John chose noon on purpose: according to Philo, the Passover sacrifices began at noon (Special Laws 2.145), though the Mishnah puts the slaughter after the afternoon offering (Pesahim 5:1). (4) A copying error between the Greek numerals for 3 and 6, suggested by some ancient writers; a few manuscripts of John do read "third" (see the variant). Augustine discussed the problem at length.

p: Pilate speaks to the accusers outside, the chief priests and their guards, who answer in 19:15.
b: The ones Pilate addresses here answer him in the next verse, and John names them: "The chief priests answered, 'We have no king except Caesar.'" So "the Jews" in this verse are the Temple leaders who brought the charge. Pilate's mocking words are aimed at them. The Jewish people as a whole were not present at the Praetorium, and the Gospel does not say they were.

a: We have no king except Caesar
p: The chief priests give up the hope of a God-sent king. Later Christians misused the line against all Jews.
b: Israel's faith held that God was its true king: Gideon refused the crown because "the LORD will rule over you" (Judges 8:23), and God told Samuel that in asking for a king the people "turned down" God (1 Samuel 8:7). The Nishmat, a Jewish prayer of uncertain date said on Sabbaths and festivals, says to God, "apart from you we have no king." So John's irony is heavy: the chief priests, guardians of the Temple, profess loyalty to Caesar alone. John names the speakers: "the chief priests," not the people. Christian preaching later turned this verse, with Matthew 27:25, into a charge against the Jewish people as a whole, a misuse that the Catholic Church and many Protestant bodies have formally rejected.

p: The condemned usually carried the crossbeam. The other Gospels say Simon of Cyrene was made to carry it.
b: A condemned man carried the crossbeam (patibulum) to the place where the upright post already stood. Matthew, Mark and Luke say the soldiers forced Simon of Cyrene to carry Jesus' cross (Mark 15:21). John says Jesus carried it "for himself." Harmonizers say Jesus began and Simon took over. Others think John left Simon out to stress that Jesus needs no help to complete his work, or to answer a later story, which Irenaeus reports, that Simon was crucified in Jesus' place. Early Christians compared Jesus to Isaac, on whom Abraham "laid" the wood for the offering (Genesis 22:6).

p: Aramaic for "skull." The traditional site lies inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
b: Gulgolta is Aramaic for "skull"; the Latin is calvaria, from which "Calvary" comes. The name may come from the shape of a rocky rise or from its use for executions. Executions took place outside the city (Hebrews 13:12; Leviticus 24:14). The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, built by Constantine in the 300s, stands on a site that was an old quarry with tombs just outside the city wall of Jesus' day, which fits John's details (19:20, 41). The "Garden Tomb" north of the Damascus Gate, proposed in the 1800s, is loved by many visitors, but archaeologists date that tomb centuries earlier.

a: Pilate wrote a sign as well
p: The Romans posted the crime of the condemned. Each Gospel gives the wording slightly differently.
b: A titulus, a board stating the charge, was sometimes hung around the neck or carried in front of a condemned man; Roman writers mention such placards, and Eusebius tells of a Christian martyr led around with one (Church History 5.1.44). The wording differs: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews" (Matthew 27:37); "The King of the Jews" (Mark 15:26); "The King of the Jews, this man" (Luke 23:38). John's is longest. The Latin initials of John's wording, INRI (Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum), are painted on many crucifixes.

a: Lots of Jews read the sign
p: Here "Jews" simply means Jewish people, as in 18:20 and 19:40. The meaning shifts within a single chapter.
b: In this verse "Jews" means ordinary Jewish people passing by the city gate, and in 19:40 it means Jewish custom: "the way Jews prepare a body for burial." Elsewhere in the same chapters the word means the chief priests (19:12–15, 21). That shift, within a few verses, is the strongest evidence that John's "the Jews" in the trial means a group of leaders, not a people. Jesus himself says that "salvation comes from the Jews" (4:22).

a: in Hebrew, in Latin and in Greek
p: Aramaic for the locals, Latin for Rome, Greek for the eastern Empire. John's readers saw a proclamation to the world.
b: Hebrew or Aramaic was the language of the land, Latin the language of Roman law and the army, and Greek the common language of the eastern Mediterranean. Multilingual notices were common in Roman Judea; the Temple's warning to Gentiles was in Greek and Latin, according to Josephus. For John, the sign becomes the first announcement of Jesus' kingship to all nations, fulfilling "I will draw everyone to myself" (12:32).

p: An unusual phrase: the chief priests of the Jewish nation, who again speak for the accusers.
b: Only here does John write "the chief priests of the Jews." The phrase sets them over against the sign's "King of the Jews": the nation's priests reject the nation's king. Here, too, "the Jews" refers to the people in whose name these priests claim to speak, while the ones acting are the priestly leaders themselves, the same group who answered "We have no king except Caesar" (19:15).

t: "What I have written, I have written"
p: The Greek perfect means a thing done that stays done. Pilate will not change the sign.
b: The KJV's "What I have written I have written" keeps the Greek form. The perfect tense gegrapha describes a past act whose result remains, so the sense is "it is written and it stays." Pilate's stubbornness may be spite toward the priests who forced his hand. John sees more: like Caiaphas, who "prophesied" without meaning to (11:51), Pilate publishes the truth about Jesus in three languages and refuses to take it back. The same perfect "written" ends the Gospel's purpose statement (20:31).

p: An expensive one-piece garment. Readers have seen in it the high priest's robe, or the unity of the church.
b: The chitōn was the long shirt worn next to the skin. Weaving one without a seam took skill. Readings: (1) The high priest's robe. Josephus says the high priest's tunic was not made of two pieces but woven as one (Jewish Antiquities 3.161), and Exodus says its opening must have a woven edge "so that it will not tear" (Exodus 28:32). If John intends this, Jesus dies as priest as well as king. (2) The church's unity. Cyprian of Carthage (about AD 251) said the untorn tunic pictures a church that must not be split, a reading tied to the untorn net of 21:11. (3) Simply history: a detail the eyewitness remembered.

a: "They divided up my clothes among themselves, and over my clothing they threw lots."
p: John quotes Psalm 22:18 word for word from its Greek translation, and sees two acts where the psalm has two lines.
b: Psalm 22 is the lament of a righteous sufferer, beginning "My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?" (Psalm 22:1). The site's Plain of Psalm 22:18 reads "They hand out my clothes among them, / and over my clothing they throw lots." John quotes the Greek of the Psalm exactly. Hebrew poetry often says one thing twice in parallel lines; John takes the two lines as two events, the clothes divided and the tunic gambled for, as Matthew does with the donkey and colt (Matthew 21:5–7). All four Gospels tell of the dividing; only John quotes the Psalm.
r: Psalm 22:18; Psalm 22:1; Psalm 22:15; Matthew 27:35; Mark 15:24; Luke 23:34

a: his mother's sister, Mary of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene
p: The Greek list can be read as three women or four. "Mary of Clopas" may be his wife, mother or daughter.
b: If "his mother's sister" and "Mary of Clopas" are one woman, there are three women; if two, there are four in two pairs, which most scholars prefer, since two sisters both named Mary is unlikely. "Mary of Clopas" means a Mary connected to Clopas, most often taken as his wife. Hegesippus, a writer of the 100s, said Clopas was the brother of Joseph, Mary's husband (in Eusebius, Church History 3.11). If the unnamed sister is Salome, the mother of Zebedee's sons (compare Mark 15:40 with Matthew 27:56), then James and John were Jesus' cousins; this is possible but not certain.
orig: Μαρία ἡ τοῦ Κλωπᾶ (Maria hē tou Klōpa)

p: Mary from Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee. Nothing in the Gospels says she was a prostitute.
b: "Magdalene" means from Magdala (Migdal), a fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, where a first-century synagogue was excavated in 2009. Luke says seven demons had gone out of her and that she helped support Jesus from her own means (Luke 8:2–3). The idea that she was a reformed prostitute comes from a sermon of Pope Gregory the Great in 591, which merged her with the sinful woman of Luke 7 and with Mary of Bethany. Eastern churches never accepted that merger, and the Catholic calendar separated the women in 1969. In John she is the first witness of the resurrection (20:11–18).

t: The disciple Jesus loved at the cross
p: The only male disciple at the cross in John. He is the witness behind 19:35.
b: In the other Gospels the male disciples have fled (Mark 14:50) and only women watch from a distance (Mark 15:40). John places the disciple Jesus loved at the foot of the cross. He is the witness of the spear and the blood and water (19:35), the first to believe at the tomb (20:8), and, according to 21:24, the source of the Gospel. On who he was, see 13:23 and the topic page on the Gospel of John.

p: "Woman" sounds cold in English. In Greek it was a polite form of address, though unusual for a son to his mother.
b: Gynai is respectful; Jesus uses it to the Samaritan woman (4:21) and to Mary Magdalene (20:15), and Greek tragedy has heroes address queens this way. Still, a son did not normally call his mother "woman," and Jesus did so only twice, at Cana (2:4) and here. The two scenes frame his ministry: at Cana his "hour" had not yet come; now it has. Many interpreters, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, see Mary here as more than a private mother: she stands for a "woman" who gives birth to a new family (compare 16:21; Genesis 3:15, 20). See the chapter page for the traditions.

a: took her into his own household
p: Literally "into his own things": his home, or his own life. Readers find a private duty, a new family, or a symbol.
b: Readings: (1) A son's duty. Jesus provides for his widowed mother, keeping the commandment to honor her (Calvin, and many Protestant interpreters). (2) A new family. At the cross Jesus creates a family of faith; the disciple and Mary become mother and son. (3) Mary as mother of believers. Origen said no one can grasp John's Gospel who has not, like this disciple, received Mary as his mother; John Paul II read "into his own" as welcoming Mary into one's inner life (Redemptoris Mater 45). (4) Symbolic figures. Rudolf Bultmann took Mary as Jewish Christianity and the disciple as Gentile Christianity. Tradition later placed Mary's last years with John at Ephesus, or in Jerusalem.

p: John says the words complete Scripture, probably Psalm 69:21, where the sufferer is given vinegar for thirst.
b: Which Scripture? Most think of Psalm 69:21, "when I was thirsty they made me drink vinegar," since sour wine follows at once; some add Psalm 22:15, "my tongue is glued to my gums." John uses an unusual verb here, teleioō, "complete, bring to its goal," rather than his usual "fulfill," and links it to "finished" (tetelestai) twice (19:28, 30). The one who offered living water (4:14; 7:37) now thirsts; and the one who said he would drink the Father's cup (18:11) drinks to the end.

p: Hyssop is a small bushy plant, an odd pole. But hyssop dipped in blood marked the doors at the first Passover.
b: Mark and Matthew say the sponge was put on a reed (Mark 15:36). Hyssop is a small herb, and a stalk long enough to reach a crucified man's mouth is hard to picture. Since the 1500s some have suggested that John wrote hyssō, "on a javelin," and a copyist misread it; the word appears in one late manuscript, apparently a correction (reported by Metzger), but almost all scholars keep "hyssop." John likely means it: Moses told Israel, "Take a bunch of hyssop and dip it into the blood" of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:22). The detail fits John's picture of Jesus as the Passover Lamb (19:36).

p: One Greek word: "it has been completed." The work the Father gave him is done.
b: Tetelestai is the perfect passive of teleō, "bring to completion": "It has been accomplished, and stands complete." It is a cry of completion, not of defeat: Jesus came to "complete" the Father's work (4:34; 17:4), and he loved his own "to the end" (telos, 13:1). A popular claim says that business receipts were stamped tetelestai meaning "paid in full." The verb was used in money matters for paying a bill, but the evidence that it was a standard receipt formula is thin, and John does not use money language here.

p: The same verb as Judas "handing over" Jesus. Here Jesus is the one who hands over, giving up his life.
b: The other Gospels say he "breathed his last" (Mark 15:37) or "gave up his spirit" (Matthew 27:50). John uses paradidōmi, the verb of "handing over" that runs through the passion (see 18:2): no one takes his life; he gives it (10:18). Some interpreters, among them Raymond Brown as a possible second meaning, hear more: Jesus "hands over the Spirit" to the believers at the cross, his mother and the beloved disciple, since the Spirit could come only when he was glorified (7:39). Most think the plain meaning is his death, with the Spirit given in 20:22.

a: the Jews did not want the bodies left
t: Keeping the law about the dead
p: The authorities ask for the bodies to come down in keeping with the law in Deuteronomy 21:22–23.
b: "The Jews" here are again the authorities who deal with Pilate. Their request is not hostile: the law commanded that the body of a hanged man must not remain overnight but be buried the same day (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), and Josephus says Jews took down even crucified criminals before sunset (Jewish War 4.317). Keeping that law before a great Sabbath was faithful observance, and it led to Jesus' burial.

a: that Sabbath was a great day
p: The Torah forbade leaving a hanged body up overnight. That Sabbath also fell on the Passover.
b: Deuteronomy says a man hanged on a tree "must not stay on the tree overnight" (Deuteronomy 21:23). Josephus notes that Jews took down the crucified and buried them before sunset (Jewish War 4.317). Romans often left bodies on crosses for days as a warning, so the request needed the governor's permission. The Sabbath was "great" because, in John's timeline, it was also the first day of the Passover festival. Breaking the legs (Latin crurifragium) hastened death, since the victim could no longer push up to breathe. The bones of a crucified man found in a Jerusalem tomb in 1968 still had a nail through the heel, but whether his legs were broken is disputed.

p: Proof of real death, a picture of baptism and the Lord's Supper, or the birth of the church from Christ's side?
b: Readings: (1) A real death. The spear proves Jesus truly died, against teachers who said Christ only seemed to suffer (compare 1 John 5:6, which insists he came through blood as well as water). Doctors have proposed fluid around the heart or lungs; a 1986 article in the Journal of the American Medical Association made this case, though medical writers disagree on details. (2) The sacraments. John Chrysostom and Augustine saw baptism (water) and the Eucharist (blood) flowing from Christ. (3) The church born from his side, as Eve was taken from Adam's side while he slept (Genesis 2:21; Augustine). (4) Living water: the fulfillment of 7:38–39.

a: The man who saw this has given testimony
p: The Gospel breaks off to vouch for what was seen. Who is "that man" who knows he speaks the truth?
b: The witness is surely the disciple Jesus loved (19:26; 21:24). The next clause is literally "and that one knows that he speaks true things." Most take "that one" as the witness himself, speaking of himself in the third person. Some, including Rudolf Bultmann, read it as an editor vouching for the witness, as "we know" does in 21:24; a few take "that one" as Christ or God, who confirms the testimony. Either way, the purpose is the purpose of the whole Gospel: "so that you may believe" (20:31). On the verb's tense, see the variant.

a: "No bone of his will be broken."
p: The Passover lamb's bones must not be broken, and God keeps the righteous one's bones. John may mean both.
b: Two texts lie behind the words. The Passover law says of the lamb, "do not break any of its bones" (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12). Psalm 34 says of the righteous person: "He keeps watch over all his bones; / not a single one gets broken" (Psalm 34:20). John's wording, "of his," is closest to the Psalm, but his whole story points to the lamb: John the Baptist called Jesus "the Lamb of God" (1:29), and Jesus dies as the lambs are slaughtered (19:14). Paul too calls Christ "our Passover lamb" (1 Corinthians 5:7).

a: "They will look at the one they pierced."
p: From Zechariah 12:10. John's Greek follows the Hebrew, not the Septuagint, which misread the verb.
b: Zechariah 12:10 tells of a day when the people of Jerusalem will mourn over one they have pierced, and God will pour out a spirit of grace and prayer. The standard Hebrew reads "they will look to me, whom they pierced"; John has "the one they pierced," and Revelation 1:7 uses the same wording: "and so will those who pierced him." The Septuagint has "they mocked" instead, apparently from misreading two Hebrew letters, so John is translating from the Hebrew or using another Greek version. In John, to "look at" the pierced one is to see and believe, as Israel looked at the bronze snake (3:14–15).

p: A council member and a secret disciple. All four Gospels give him the burial.
b: Mark calls Joseph an honored council member who was looking for God's kingdom (Mark 15:43); Matthew calls him rich (Matthew 27:57); Luke says he had not agreed with the council's decision (Luke 23:51). Arimathea may be Ramathaim, Samuel's hometown (1 Samuel 1:1). John calls him a secret disciple, like the leaders who believed but feared being put out of the synagogue (12:42). Asking Pilate for the body of an executed rebel was a public act; in John, Joseph and Nicodemus finally come into the light. A Roman burial for the condemned was not guaranteed, so Joseph's request mattered.

p: Joseph was himself a Jew. He feared the authorities, as people in 7:13, 9:22 and 12:42 did.
b: Joseph from Arimathea was a Jew, and in Mark a member of the council (Mark 15:43). His fear was of the authorities who could expel Jesus' followers from the synagogue (9:22; 12:42). John uses the same phrase of Jews in Jerusalem in 7:13, and of the disciples in 20:19. In each case the people afraid are Jews, and what they fear is the leaders, which shows how John uses the word.

a: Nicodemus came too, the man who had first come to Jesus at night
p: The Pharisee who came by night (3:2) and defended Jesus' right to a hearing (7:50) now comes in daylight to bury him.
b: Nicodemus appears only in John. He came to Jesus at night with questions (3:1–2), later asked the council to hear Jesus before judging him (7:50–51), and now joins Joseph openly. Readers have long debated whether he ever became a full believer. John does not say, but his gift speaks loudly. The words about coming to the light in 3:21 seem to find their answer here.

p: A Roman pound (litra) was about 12 ounces, so this was some 75 pounds of spices: an amount fit for a king.
b: The litra, the Roman pound, weighed about 327 grams, so a hundred of them came to about 33 kilograms or 75 of our pounds. That is a huge amount. Myrrh was a fragrant resin, and aloes here is probably powdered aloeswood (eaglewood), a fragrant resin-filled wood. Royal burials used great quantities of spices: King Asa was laid on a couch "filled with spices, all kinds of them" (2 Chronicles 16:14), and Josephus says hundreds of servants carried spices at Herod's funeral (Jewish Antiquities 17.199). John, who has called Jesus king throughout the trial, now shows him buried as one.

p: The body was wrapped with spices in linen. Jews buried quickly, usually the same day, in rock-cut family tombs.
b: Othonia can be strips or sheets of linen; Mark speaks of a single linen cloth (sindōn, Mark 15:46). Jews did not embalm like Egyptians; spices honored the dead and masked the smell. Bodies were laid in rock-cut tombs, and a year later the bones were often gathered into a bone box, an ossuary. In Mark and Luke the women come on Sunday to anoint the body (Mark 16:1), as if it had not been done; John's account suggests a full burial was given in haste. The Shroud of Turin, claimed as Jesus' burial cloth, was dated by radiocarbon tests in 1988 to the Middle Ages, though some dispute the tests.

a: a new tomb, where nobody had been placed yet
p: The tomb was unused, so no one could confuse Jesus' body with another.
b: Matthew says the tomb was Joseph's own, newly cut from rock (Matthew 27:60); Luke, like John, says no one had yet been laid in it (Luke 23:53). An unused tomb meant the body was not mixed with others, which matters for the empty tomb (20:1–8). Christians have connected this with the servant of Isaiah 53:9, whose grave was set beside the rich when he died. The garden ties the end of the passion to its beginning (18:1).

a: on the first day of the week
p: Literally "on day one of the Sabbaths," a Jewish way to say Sunday. Christians soon met on this day.
b: Jews named weekdays by counting from the Sabbath: "day one of the week" was Sunday. All four Gospels place the discovery of the empty tomb on this day. John marks it again in 20:19 and has Jesus return "after eight days" (20:26), counting inclusively, on the next Sunday. Early Christians gathered on the first day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2) and called it "the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10). Whether Sunday worship replaced the Sabbath or stands beside it is a question on which churches differ; see the topic on the Sabbath.
orig: τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων (tē mia tōn sabbatōn)

p: Mark says the sun had risen. John says it was still dark, and in John darkness often means more than the hour.
b: Mark has the women come "with the sun now up" (Mark 16:2); Matthew says "as light was breaking" (Matthew 28:1). John's "still dark" may simply mean very early. But John uses darkness as a sign: Judas went out "and it was night" (13:30), Nicodemus came at night (3:2), and the light shines in the darkness (1:5). Mary comes in the dark, not yet knowing what has happened. In John she seems to come alone, though her "we" in 20:2 hints at the other women the Synoptics name.

a: to the other disciple, whom Jesus loved
p: Here the verb is phileō; elsewhere it is agapaō for the same disciple. John uses both freely.
b: Everywhere else the disciple "whom Jesus loved" is described with agapaō (13:23; 19:26; 21:7, 20). Here John uses phileō. He does the same with Lazarus (11:3 phileō, 11:5 agapaō) and with the Father's love for the Son (3:35 agapaō, 5:20 phileō). This matters for 21:15–17, where some preachers build a great deal on the difference between the two verbs. John's own usage suggests he treats them as near twins.
orig: ὃν ἐφίλει ὁ Ἰησοῦς (hon ephilei ho Iēsous)

a: They have carried the Lord away from the tomb
p: Mary first thinks of grave robbers, a real fear then. Matthew reports a rumor that the disciples stole the body.
b: Tombs were robbed for valuables or for spite. A marble slab known as the Nazareth Inscription, sent to Paris "from Nazareth" in 1878, records an imperial edict threatening death for disturbing tombs or moving bodies. A 2020 study traced its marble to the island of Kos, so it probably has nothing to do with Galilee or Jesus. Matthew says the chief priests spread the story that the disciples stole the body (Matthew 28:13–15). John answers that rumor indirectly: the grave cloths left neatly in place (20:6–7) are not what thieves would leave.

a: The other disciple sped ahead, faster than Peter
p: The beloved disciple arrives first; Peter goes in first. Readers have seen rivalry, respect, or only vivid memory.
b: Luke briefly tells of Peter running to the tomb (Luke 24:12) and of "some" who went (Luke 24:24). John adds the other disciple. In John the two often appear together (13:23–26; 18:15–16; 21:7, 20–23), and the beloved disciple is always a step ahead in insight. Readings: (1) Two traditions honored side by side, Peter's leadership and the beloved disciple's witness (Raymond Brown); (2) quiet rivalry between churches that looked to Peter and the community that looked to this disciple; (3) plain eyewitness memory. Notice that the younger runner waits, and Peter enters first.

a: rolled up separately in one place
p: The cloths lie in order, not thrown aside. Lazarus came out still wrapped; Jesus left his wrappings behind.
b: The head cloth (soudarion, from Latin sudarium, "sweat cloth") is the same item that bound Lazarus's face (11:44). Lazarus walked out still wrapped and would die again; Jesus has left death's clothing behind. John Chrysostom noted that thieves would not stop to unwrap a body soaked in myrrh and then fold the cloths. "Rolled up" (entetyligmenon) may also mean "wrapped around," keeping its shape. A story often repeated online, that a folded napkin at a Jewish meal meant "I will return," has no evidence behind it.

p: Most think he believed Jesus had risen. Augustine thought he only believed Mary's report that the body was gone.
b: Most interpreters take "he believed" in John's full sense: from the empty tomb and the cloths, he believed Jesus had risen, the first in the Gospel to do so. But 20:9 says they did not yet understand the Scripture, and the disciples go home without telling anyone. Augustine therefore thought he believed only that the body had been taken, as Mary said. Most modern commentators answer that the disciple believed without yet understanding the Scriptures, which is why 20:9 begins "for": belief came by seeing before it came by Scripture. He becomes a model for readers who believe without seeing the Lord (20:29).

a: the Scripture that says he had to rise from the dead
p: John does not say which passage. Early Christians pointed to Psalm 16, Hosea 6, Jonah and Isaiah 53.
b: The New Testament often says the Messiah "had to" (dei) rise "according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:4; Luke 24:46) without naming a text. Peter in Acts quotes Psalm 16:10, "you will not allow your loyal one to see the Pit," in its Greek form, "to see decay" (Acts 2:27–31). Others pointed to Hosea's hope of being raised up on the third day (Hosea 6:2), to Jonah's three days (Matthew 12:40) and to the servant who lives after his suffering (Isaiah 53:10–12). Jewish interpreters read these passages differently: of Israel's restoration, of David, or of the righteous generally. John's point is that understanding came only after the resurrection (2:22).
r: Psalm 16:10; Hosea 6:2; Jonah 1:17; Isaiah 53:10–12; Luke 24:25–27; Luke 24:44–46; Acts 2:24–32; 1 Corinthians 15:4; 2:22

a: seated one by the head and one by the feet
p: The Gospels differ on the angels. Some readers see in John's scene the two cherubim on the ark's lid.
b: Mark has one young man in white sitting inside the tomb (Mark 16:5), Matthew one angel on the stone (Matthew 28:2), Luke two men (Luke 24:4), John two angels seated at either end of the place where the body had been. Some interpreters, both ancient and modern, see the two cherubim at each end of the atonement lid on the ark of the covenant: "their faces turned toward the lid" (Exodus 25:20), the place where God met Israel. The comparison is suggestive, not stated. The differences in number are the kind found in independent reports of the same event.

a: she did not know it was Jesus
p: The risen Jesus is often not known at first. Grief, early light, a changed body, or God's timing?
b: Mary, the disciples on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:16), and the fishermen by the lake (21:4) all fail at first to recognize Jesus. Explanations: grief and tears, the dim light, a body changed in its new life (Paul's "spiritual body," 1 Corinthians 15:44), or God holding back recognition until the right moment (Luke 24:16 says "their eyes were kept" from knowing him). In John, recognition comes when he speaks her name, as the shepherd "calls out to his own sheep, each by name" (10:3).

a: the man who kept the garden
p: Mary's mistake is half true. Readers have seen Jesus as the new Adam in a new Eden.
b: Kēpouros means a garden keeper. Mary's guess fits the setting (19:41), but Christian readers since the early church have seen more: the first man was put in a garden "to work it and to guard it" (Genesis 2:15), and now the risen Jesus stands in a garden on the first day of a new creation. Some even painted him with a gardener's spade. The gardener also appears in an early anti-Christian story: Tertullian (about AD 200) mocks those who said the gardener had moved the body so visitors would not trample his lettuces (On the Spectacles 30), which shows the claim was in circulation.

p: An Aramaic form of "rabbi": "my master, my teacher." She knows him when he speaks her name.
b: Rabbouni (Aramaic rabbuni) is a heightened form of "rabbi," used also by blind Bartimaeus (Mark 10:51). It literally means "my great one, my master," and John translates it "Teacher." Mary may be returning to the relationship she had before, which explains Jesus' next words (20:17). The moment fulfills the shepherd saying: "He calls out to his own sheep, each by name... The sheep follow him, because his voice is familiar to them" (10:3–4). On "in Hebrew," see the note on 19:13.

p: The KJV's "Touch me not" suggests he could not be touched. The Greek means "Stop holding on to me."
b: Mē mou haptou is a present imperative with "not": it usually means stop doing something already going on. Mary has taken hold of him, as the women do in Matthew 28:9, who "took hold of his feet." The Latin Noli me tangere and the KJV's "Touch me not" made it sound as if touching was forbidden, which clashes with his invitation to Thomas a week later (20:27). Readings of the reason: (1) Jesus must go to the Father, and their relationship will now be through the Spirit, not his physical presence (16:7); (2) she should not try to hold on to the past; (3) she has a message to deliver, so go. Most commentators combine (1) and (3).

p: For the first time Jesus calls the disciples his brothers. Hebrews links the words to Psalm 22:22.
b: Jesus had called the disciples friends (15:15); now, after the cross, they are brothers, sharing his Father. Matthew has the risen Jesus say the same (Matthew 28:10). Hebrews quotes the Psalm that John has already used at the cross: "I will spread the news of your name to my brothers" (Psalm 22:22; Hebrews 2:12). The second half of Psalm 22 turns from suffering to praise; Christians have read it as the resurrection half of the Psalm.

a: my Father and your Father, my God and your God
p: A new bond: his Father is now theirs. But why "my God and your God"? Readers have read it in different ways.
b: The words may echo Ruth's promise of belonging, "your God is my God" (Ruth 1:16): Jesus' Father and God becomes the disciples' Father and God. But he does not say "our Father": he keeps a difference between his sonship and theirs. Arians in the 300s, and Jehovah's Witnesses today, take "my God" as proof that Jesus is less than God. Nicene writers such as Gregory of Nazianzus answered that Jesus speaks of "my God" as a man and "my Father" as the eternal Son. A few verses later Thomas calls Jesus "my God" (20:28), and John lets both statements stand.

p: A woman is the first to see the risen Jesus and to announce it: an "apostle to the apostles."
b: In John, Matthew and the later ending of Mark (16:9), Mary Magdalene is the first to see the risen Jesus. "I have seen the Lord" is the formula of an apostle's witness (compare 1 Corinthians 9:1). Josephus says women's testimony was not accepted in Jewish courts (Jewish Antiquities 4.219), and Paul's list of witnesses leaves the women out (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). Many historians argue that no one inventing the story would make women the first witnesses. Hippolytus of Rome (early 200s), in a commentary on the Song of Songs that survives in Georgian, says Christ sent the women (whom he names Martha and Mary) as apostles to the apostles; medieval writers gave the title to Mary Magdalene herself, and in 2016 the Catholic Church raised her memorial day to a feast with that title.

a: The doors of the place where the disciples were staying were locked
p: The risen body can be touched and carries wounds, yet locked doors do not stop it.
b: John stresses both sides: Jesus shows his hands and side (20:20), invites Thomas to touch (20:27), and eats by the lake (21:13); yet he appears inside a locked room. Luke does the same (Luke 24:36–43). Christian teaching has drawn from this that the resurrection body is the same body, transformed, what Paul calls a "spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:44). Some critical scholars think the two emphases reflect early debates, one side stressing that it was really him, the other that he was not merely a revived corpse.

a: because they were afraid of the Jews
p: The frightened disciples were Jews themselves. "The Jews" here means the authorities who had just had Jesus killed.
b: Everyone in this room is Jewish. So "the Jews" cannot mean the Jewish people as such; it means the Jerusalem authorities who had arranged Jesus' death and might come next for his followers (as in 7:13; 9:22; 19:38). The terms used on this site keep John's own word, "the Jews," so that readers can see what he wrote, with notes like this one where it means the leaders. Adele Reinhartz and others argue that John's way of speaking still shaped later hostility toward Jews as a whole, and that readers must name that history honestly.

p: The everyday Jewish greeting, shalom aleichem. After the cross it becomes a gift as well.
b: "Peace to you" is the normal Hebrew and Aramaic greeting, shalom aleichem, still used today. On Jesus' lips after the resurrection it also fulfills his promises to leave them his peace (14:27; 16:33). He says it three times in this chapter (20:19, 21, 26). To disciples who had abandoned him, the first word is not blame but peace.

a: Just as the Father has sent me out, I too am sending you
p: The church's mission is modeled on Jesus' own. John uses two verbs for "send" without much difference.
b: Jesus calls the Father "the one who sent me" more than forty times in John. Now he hands that mission on, as he prayed he would (17:18). The Greek uses apostellō (from which "apostle") for the Father's sending and pempō for his own; John uses the two interchangeably elsewhere (compare 5:36 and 5:37). This is John's version of the commission that ends Matthew (Matthew 28:19–20) and begins Acts (Acts 1:8).

p: The same rare verb is used when God breathed life into the first human. Ezekiel's dry bones are another echo.
b: Emphysaō, "breathe into," appears only here in the New Testament. The Greek of Genesis 2:7 uses it when the LORD God "blew into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being." In Ezekiel 37:9 the prophet calls the wind to "breathe on" the dead so that they live. In both Hebrew and Greek the same word means breath, wind and spirit (ruach, pneuma; compare 3:8). John is showing a new creation: the risen Jesus breathes God's life into his people, as the Creator did at the beginning.

p: In John the Spirit is given on Easter evening; in Acts, fifty days later. How do the two fit?
b: Views: (1) Two tellings of one gift. John and Luke each tell the giving of the Spirit in their own way; John ties it to the resurrection (Raymond Brown and many others). (2) A first gift and a fuller one. Easter gives the Spirit for new life or for the apostles' office; Pentecost gives power for public mission (Calvin; many evangelicals). (3) An acted promise. The breath was a sign of what would come at Pentecost (Theodore of Mopsuestia; D. A. Carson). (4) Pentecostal teaching sees two works: new birth by the Spirit, then the baptism in the Spirit for power (Acts 1:8). Theodore's view was condemned at the Council of Constantinople in 553, but versions of it are held today.

a: those sins have been forgiven them
p: The Greek perfect has sparked a long debate: do the disciples forgive, or do they announce what God has already done?
b: Both verbs in the result clauses are perfect passives: "have been forgiven," "have been held." Julius Mantey argued in 1939 that this means the disciples only declare a forgiveness God has already granted; Henry Cadbury replied the same year that a perfect in such a sentence normally states the sure result ("they are thereby forgiven"), not prior time. The passive points to God as the one who forgives (Mark 2:7). Whom did Jesus address: the apostles as church leaders, or all the disciples present (Luke 24:33 has others in the room)? How churches answer shapes their practice of confession; see the chapter page. The debate assumes the perfect that NA28 and SBLGNT print; the Tyndale House edition and the Byzantine text do not print a perfect here (see the variant).
r: Matthew 16:19; Matthew 18:18; Mark 2:7; Luke 24:47; Acts 2:38; James 5:16

p: "Thomas" is Aramaic for "twin"; Didymus is the Greek word for it. We never learn whose twin he was.
b: Te'oma in Aramaic and didymos in Greek both mean "twin." John gives both names three times (11:16; 20:24; 21:2). Thomas is no stranger to bold loyalty: he urged the others to go and die with Jesus (11:16), and he asked the honest question of how they could know the way (14:5). In Syriac tradition he is "Judas Thomas," and some later writings made him Jesus' twin, an idea with no support in the Gospels. Tradition says he took the gospel east, to Persia and India.

a: the print of the nails in his hands
p: Only John mentions nails in the hands; Luke implies hands and feet. Romans used both ropes and nails.
b: Victims were tied or nailed to the cross. The heel bone of a crucified man named Yehohanan, found in a Jerusalem tomb in 1968, still had an iron nail through it, which shows nailing was used in Jesus' time and place. The Greek cheir, "hand," can include the wrist, and some argue nails went through the wrist, since the palm might tear; others reply that ropes bore the weight. Christians have connected the wounds with the Hebrew of Psalm 22:16, which reads in some ancient witnesses "they pierced my hands and my feet," a famous textual crux.

p: Counting both ends, "after eight days" means the next Sunday. Early Christians called Sunday "the eighth day."
b: Ancient counting included the first and last days, so "after eight days" is our "a week later": the following Sunday. Jesus meets the disciples again on the first day of the week, and the church began to gather on that day. The Epistle of Barnabas (about AD 130) calls Sunday "the eighth day," the beginning of a new world (Epistle of Barnabas 15:9), and Justin Martyr says the same.

a: Do not turn into an unbeliever. Be a believer.
p: The Greek words mean "unbelieving" and "believing," not "doubting." And John never says Thomas touched.
b: Apistos and pistos are "unbelieving" and "believing" (or "faithful"); the English nickname "Doubting Thomas" and translations that say "stop doubting" soften the contrast into a mood. Jesus is calling Thomas to a decision. Painters, most famously Caravaggio, show Thomas putting his finger into the wound, but the text does not say he did. His answer comes in words, not in touching (20:28), and Jesus says, "you have believed because you have seen me" (20:29), not "because you touched."
orig: μὴ γίνου ἄπιστος ἀλλὰ πιστός (mē ginou apistos alla pistos)

p: The Gospel's highest confession, spoken to Jesus. It answers the Gospel's first verse: "the Word was God."
b: The Greek uses the nominative with the article, common for addressing someone ("the Lord of me"). "Said to him" shows the words are spoken to Jesus. The pairing echoes Psalm 35:23, where the psalmist calls on "my God and my Lord." With 1:1 and 1:18, it frames the Gospel with Jesus called God. Theodore of Mopsuestia, and in modern times some others, read the words as an exclamation of praise to the Father; most interpreters reject that because of "said to him." Jehovah's Witnesses accept that Thomas addressed Jesus but understand "god" as "a mighty one." Suetonius says the emperor Domitian liked to be called "our Lord and God" (Domitian 13), so John's first readers may have heard a challenge to Rome.
orig: Ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου (Ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou)

a: Blessed are the ones who did not see, and yet believed
p: A blessing for every later reader. Faith without sight is not second-class.
b: Thomas sees and believes; later disciples will believe through the apostles' word (17:20). Peter writes to such readers, who love Jesus without having seen him (1 Peter 1:8). The verbs are past tense ("did not see... believed"), as if spoken from the viewpoint of the Gospel's readers, who have already believed. The next verses tell those readers that this book was written for them.

p: John calls Jesus' miracles "signs": acts that point beyond themselves to who he is.
b: John counts Jesus' first two signs (2:11; 4:54) and tells seven in all before the cross, by most counts: water into wine, the official's son, the man at Bethesda, the feeding, the walking on water, the man born blind, and Lazarus. Some add the catch of fish in chapter 21. A sign (sēmeion) is meant to be read, not only marveled at. Many scholars think John used an earlier written collection of signs (the "signs source"), which may have ended with words like 20:30–31; others think the Gospel was written as one piece.

t: Written to win new believers, or to strengthen believers?
p: The Gospel's purpose statement. Its verb tense is debated, and so is its audience.
b: Was John written to bring outsiders to faith, or to help Christians keep believing? The manuscripts differ between a present-tense verb ("believe," keep on believing) and an aorist ("come to believe"); see the variant. D. A. Carson argues that the purpose is evangelistic either way, perhaps aimed at Jews and converts to Judaism in the Greek-speaking world; Raymond Brown and many others think the Gospel was written mainly for a Christian community under pressure. The content of faith is exact: that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, the very confession Martha made (11:27).

a: the Messiah, the Son of God
p: Two titles: the Jewish hope (anointed king) and the Son of God, which in John means more than a royal title.
b: Christos translates Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one." In Israel's Scriptures the king of David's line was God's "son": "You are my son. This day I have fathered you" (Psalm 2:7; 2 Samuel 7:14). So "Messiah, Son of God" could be one royal idea, as when Nathanael calls Jesus both Son of God and King of Israel (1:49). John means more: the Son who is "one" with the Father (10:30) and who was "with God" in the beginning (1:1).
orig: ὁ χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ (ho christos ho huios tou theou)

p: 20:30–31 sounds like an ending, and then the story goes on. Who added chapter 21, and why?
b: Most scholars think chapter 21 was added after the Gospel was first finished, because 20:30–31 reads like a conclusion and 21:24 speaks of the disciple in the third person with a "we." Views: (1) A later epilogue by the author's circle, written after the beloved disciple died, to explain his death (21:23) and Peter's (Bultmann, Brown and many others); (2) an epilogue by the author himself, added later; (3) part of the original plan, balancing the prologue of 1:1–18 (Richard Bauckham, Paul Minear). The vocabulary and style are close to the rest of John. No surviving manuscript of John ends at 20:31.

p: The Sea of Galilee, named after the city of Tiberias that Herod Antipas built on its shore around AD 20.
b: The lake is called the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 4:18), the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1), and, by John alone in the New Testament, the Sea of Tiberias (6:1). Herod Antipas founded Tiberias around AD 20 and named it after the emperor Tiberius; the lake's new name took hold over the following decades, which some see as a sign of John's later date.
