Galilee is where the disciples were first called, and where Matthew and Mark say the risen Jesus would meet them (Matthew 28:7; Mark 16:7).

t: Zebedee's sons, and two unnamed disciples
p: The only mention of James and John in this Gospel. The beloved disciple must be one of the seven, but which?
b: John's Gospel mentions "Zebedee's sons" only here, and never names James or John at all. The disciple Jesus loved is in the boat (21:7), so he is one of these seven. Tradition (Irenaeus and most readers since) takes him to be John son of Zebedee. Others note that the list ends with "two more of his disciples," unnamed, and suggest the beloved disciple was one of them, someone outside the Twelve; Richard Bauckham argues for John the Elder, a Jerusalem disciple mentioned by Papias. The question is open; see 13:23.

p: A return to the old life after failure, or simply men who needed food while they waited?
b: Readings: (1) A step back. After the resurrection appearances, the disciples go back to their old trade, as if unsure what comes next; the empty night of fishing shows that without Jesus they can do nothing (15:5). (2) Nothing wrong. They were in Galilee, as Matthew and Mark say they were told to be, and they needed to eat. (3) A sign of mission. Jesus had called them to fish for people (Mark 1:17); the great catch that follows pictures the church's mission. Luke tells a similar miraculous catch at the start of Jesus' ministry (Luke 5:1–11); some think the two are one tradition told in different places.

a: you have no fish to eat, do you?
p: Prosphagion is anything eaten with bread, which in Galilee usually meant fish.
b: Prosphagion means a relish, the thing you eat with your bread, and around the lake that was usually fish. The question is shaped to expect "no." Jesus addresses them as paidia, "children" or "boys," a friendly, informal word a man on shore might shout to young fishermen. He used the warmer teknia, "little children," at the supper (13:33).
orig: μή τι προσφάγιον ἔχετε; (mē ti prosphagion echete?)

a: Throw the net over on the boat's right-hand side
p: Someone on shore can sometimes see a shoal that people in a boat cannot. The size of the catch is the sign.
b: Galilean fishermen worked at night with a cast net or a trammel net, and sold their fish in the morning. A person standing on the shore, higher up, can sometimes see a school of fish near the surface. So the instruction itself need not be miraculous; the size of the catch is what tells the disciple it is the Lord (21:7). The "right side" may hint at the right as the side of favor, but John does not explain it.

t: Why put clothes on to swim?
p: Gymnos means naked or only lightly dressed. Peter, oddly, ties on his outer coat before jumping in.
b: Gymnos can mean fully naked or stripped down to a loincloth or undershirt, as men worked in the heat. Peter "tied his outer coat around himself" (diezōsato, the same root as "belt" in 21:18) before jumping in. The likely reason is respect: to greet anyone, let alone the Lord, a Jew should be decently dressed. Some readers see an echo of Adam and Eve, who covered themselves before God after their sin (Genesis 3:7–10); Peter, who denied Jesus, rushes toward him anyway.

p: The same word as the fire where Peter denied Jesus (18:18). Breakfast is ready before they bring their catch.
b: See the note on 18:18. Jesus has already prepared fish and bread, the same two foods as at the feeding of the five thousand (6:9–11). He does not need their catch, yet he asks for some (21:10): their work is welcomed into his meal.

p: The exact count has invited many explanations, from fish species to number puzzles, or just a careful count.
b: Proposals: (1) All kinds of fish, all nations. Jerome said Greek zoologists counted 153 kinds of fish, so the catch stands for every people (Commentary on Ezekiel 47); no surviving zoologist gives that exact figure, though Oppian's poem on fishing is often cited. (2) A triangle number. Augustine noted that 153 is the sum of 1 to 17, and found meaning in 17 (Tractates on John 122). (3) Ezekiel's river. J. A. Emerton noted that the letters of En-gedi and En-eglaim, the places where fishermen spread nets in Ezekiel 47:10, add up in Hebrew to 17 and 153. (4) Simply a count, remembered because fishermen counted their catch to divide it. Richard Bauckham finds several number patterns combined.

p: The verb is the root of "schism." The net holds everyone, like the soldiers' untorn tunic.
b: In Luke's catch the nets began to tear (Luke 5:6). Here the net holds. John uses the verb schizō for the tunic the soldiers would not tear (19:24), and its noun schisma for the "division" Jesus caused in crowds (7:43; 9:16; 10:19). Many readers, from Cyprian and Augustine to modern commentators, take the untorn net as a picture of the one church gathering people of every kind without splitting, in line with Jesus' prayer "so that all of them will be one" (17:21).

a: took the bread and handed it to them
t: A meal with the risen Lord
p: The words recall the feeding of the five thousand and the Lord's Supper.
b: The phrasing follows the feeding of the five thousand, when "Jesus took the loaves" and passed them around (6:11) and the words at the Last Supper in the other Gospels (Mark 14:22). Luke tells how the Emmaus disciples knew Jesus when he broke the bread (Luke 24:35), and Peter later says the apostles shared meals with him after he rose (Acts 10:41). Many readers see a eucharistic meaning; others think John simply shows the risen Jesus caring for his friends.

p: John counts the appearances to the disciples: Easter evening, a week later, and now. Mary's meeting is not counted.
b: The count includes only appearances to the group: 20:19–23 and 20:26–29, then this one. The meeting with Mary Magdalene (20:14–17) was to one person, not "to the disciples." Counting is a habit of John's: he numbers the first two signs (2:11; 4:54), and Peter's three denials are now answered by three questions.

a: do you love me more than these?
p: The Greek can mean "more than these men love me," "more than you love them," or "more than these things."
b: Pleon toutōn is ambiguous. (1) "More than these other disciples love me." Peter had boasted that even if all others fell away, he would not (Mark 14:29; compare John 13:37). This is the most common view. (2) "More than you love these men." Possible, but less natural. (3) "More than these things": the boat, the nets, the fishing life he had just gone back to. The English keeps the ambiguity of the Greek. Notice that Peter does not compare himself with anyone in his answer.
orig: ἀγαπᾷς με πλέον τούτων; (agapas me pleon toutōn?)

a: you yourself know that I love you
p: Jesus asks with agapaō twice, then phileō; Peter answers with phileō each time. Does the change mean something?
b: Jesus asks agapas me? twice and phileis me? the third time; Peter answers philō se all three times. Views: (1) A real difference. Agapaō is the higher, self-giving love; Peter, humbled, will claim only the affection of a friend, until Jesus comes down to his word (B. F. Westcott, and popular preaching; Richard Trench had argued the reverse, that phileō is the warmer word, which shows how unstable the distinction is). (2) Synonyms. John uses the two verbs interchangeably (3:35 and 5:20; 11:3 and 11:5; 20:2 and 13:23); the Greek translation of the Old Testament does too; and the passage also varies "feed/shepherd," "lambs/sheep," and two verbs for "know." Peter is hurt by the third asking, not by a change of verb (21:17). Most modern scholars, such as Carson and Brown, hold view (2). Augustine held it too.

p: Jesus, the good shepherd (10:11), now gives Peter the shepherd's work. Peter later urges church elders to do the same.
b: The three commands vary: "feed" (boske) my lambs, "shepherd" (poimaine) my sheep, "feed" my sheep. The flock remains "mine": Jesus does not hand over ownership. In Ezekiel 34 God condemns Israel's shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock and promises to shepherd the sheep himself. 1 Peter, written in Peter's name, has him urge church elders, as their fellow elder, to tend God's flock willingly (1 Peter 5:1–2). What this commission means for Peter's later role, and for any successors, is one of the deepest divides among churches; see the chapter page.

a: It hurt Peter that he asked him the third time
p: Three times by one charcoal fire Peter said "I am not." Three times by another he says "I love you."
b: Augustine and John Chrysostom both saw the threefold question as undoing the threefold denial (18:17, 25–27): "a threefold confession for a threefold denial," as Augustine put it. The setting matches: a charcoal fire then (18:18) and a charcoal fire now (21:9). Peter is grieved because the third question reminds him of his third denial, or because it seems to doubt him. His answer appeals to what Jesus knows, not to his own feelings: "you know all there is to know."

a: you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will tie a belt on you and take you where you do not want to go
p: John explains this as a prediction of Peter's martyrdom. Early tradition says he was crucified in Rome under Nero.
b: "Stretch out your hands" was a way of describing crucifixion in ancient writers, and Christian writers took it so. 1 Clement (about AD 96) says Peter suffered and bore witness, without naming the place or manner (1 Clement 5:4). Tertullian (about AD 200) says Peter was "bound to the cross" in Rome (Scorpiace 15). Eusebius reports Origen's statement that Peter was crucified head downward at his own request (Church History 3.1), a story also told in the Acts of Peter. Some read the order of the clauses (hands stretched out before being "belted") as a sign that it describes old age generally, but John's comment in 21:19 settles what he meant.

p: The first call (1:43) is renewed. Earlier Peter could not follow yet (13:36). Now he will, to the death.
b: At the supper Jesus told Peter that he could not follow him now but would follow later (13:36), and Peter said he would lay down his life (13:37), then failed. Here the word is spoken again after the prophecy of his death: following now means following Jesus to a cross. The present tense of the next "follow me" (21:22) means "keep following."

a: who had leaned back against Jesus' chest at the supper
p: John recalls 13:23–25 to identify the disciple. His closeness to Jesus echoes the Son's closeness to the Father (1:18).
b: The disciple is identified by the scene at the supper, where he reclined next to Jesus and asked who would hand him over (13:23–25). The image of resting on Jesus' chest recalls the prologue, which places the Son at the Father's side, literally in his bosom (1:18). The one who was nearest to Jesus is presented as the reliable witness who stands behind this book (21:24).

a: Suppose I want him to remain until I come
p: A rumor said this disciple would live until Jesus returned. The Gospel corrects it, perhaps after he had died.
b: "Until I come" refers to Jesus' return (14:3). Some early Christians expected the end within their lifetime (Mark 9:1; 1 Thessalonians 4:15). If a rumor said the beloved disciple would not die before then, his death would shake people's faith. Many scholars think 21:23 was written soon after he died, to show that Jesus never promised it. Others think he was still alive and very old, and the correction was made while he lived. Either way, the point to Peter is: your calling is yours; follow me.

p: A name for the believers as a family. In Greek the plural includes sisters too.
b: Jesus had called the disciples "my brothers" (20:17); now "the brothers" is a name for the whole Christian community, as in Acts 1:15 and the letters of John (3 John 3). Greek used the masculine plural adelphoi for a mixed group, so "brothers and sisters" is the meaning. Some translations write that out; this site keeps "brothers" with this note.

a: the one who wrote them down
t: Who wrote it, and who are "we"?
p: The disciple both testified and "wrote." Did he write it himself, or cause it to be written? Others add "we know."
b: "Wrote" can mean "wrote personally" or "had written": Pilate "wrote" the sign (19:19) though someone else surely lettered it. So the verse fits both the traditional view that the beloved disciple wrote the Gospel and the view that his testimony was written down by others. The "we" who vouch for him may be the church leaders who published the book (an editor's note), or, as Richard Bauckham argues, the author himself speaking with the "we" of authoritative testimony, as in 3 John 12. Irenaeus (about AD 180) says John, the Lord's disciple who leaned on his breast, published the Gospel at Ephesus (Against Heresies 3.1.1).
orig: ὁ γράψας ταῦτα, καὶ οἴδαμεν (ho grapsas tauta, kai oidamen)

a: I do not think the world itself would have space
p: A deliberate exaggeration, common in ancient writing. The Gospel ends by admitting how much it left out.
b: The last voice is singular, "I do not think" (oimai), after the "we" of 21:24, perhaps the final editor. The overstatement was a familiar way to end a book. Jewish teachers later used similar images: a saying credited to Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai says that if all the heavens were parchment and all the trees pens, they could not hold all he had learned. The ending matches 20:30: John chose. What is written is enough to believe and to have life (20:31), but it does not exhaust who Jesus is.
